renal-33.q: Leakage with coughing or sneezing in a multiparous woman is:
renal-33.e: Outlet incompetence from pelvic floor weakness; treat with pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, weight loss.

renal-33.q: Urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity is treated with:
renal-33.e: Overflow incontinence (incomplete emptying) uses catheterization; bethanechol helps an underactive detrusor.
Bladder overfills and dribbles, e.g., BPH, diabetic neuropathy.

renal-33.q: A spinal cord transection above the sacral segments produces after spinal shock:
renal-33.e: Sacral reflex intact but no brain control (Guyton).

renal-47.q: Which diuretic class acts on the thick ascending limb?
renal-47.e: PCT: acetazolamide; TAL: loops (NKCC2); DCT: thiazides (NCC); collecting duct: K⁺-sparing.

o: Proximal tubule and thin descending limb
renal-47.e: It is filtered but not reabsorbed, so it holds water in the tubule by osmotic effect.

renal-47.q: Which diuretic acts on the collecting duct?
Loop diuretics produce the greatest natriuresis because the TAL:
renal-47.e: Up to 20–30% of filtered Na⁺ can be excreted.

renal-48.e: It first expands ECF volume, which can precipitate pulmonary edema; also contraindicated in anuria.
Osmotic agent draws water out of tissues.

o: Raising tubular fluid osmolarity, limiting water reabsorption

renal-48.q: A serious adverse effect of mannitol is:
renal-48.e: Contraindicated in anuria and heart failure.

renal-49.q: Acetazolamide is used for all EXCEPT:
renal-49.e: Also used for metabolic alkalosis; side effects include paresthesias, NH₃ toxicity and sulfa allergy.

renal-49.q: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase mainly in the:

renal-49.e: Metabolic acidosis stimulates ventilation; also glaucoma.

renal-50.e: Abolishes the medullary gradient; also stimulates PGE release (blunted by NSAIDs).

renal-50.q: Which effect of loop diuretics is used to treat hypercalcemia?
renal-50.e: Loops lose calcium (Loops Lose Ca²⁺); thiazides do the opposite. Toxicities: Ototoxicity, Hypokalemia, Hypomagnesemia, Dehydration, Allergy (sulfa), Alkalosis, Nephritis, Gout (OHH DAANG).

renal-50.q: A patient with a sulfa allergy needs a loop diuretic. Best choice:
renal-50.e: Ethacrynic acid is not a sulfonamide but is more ototoxic and can cause hyperuricemia.

renal-51.q: Thiazides are useful in calcium stones because they:
renal-51.e: Increased Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the DCT; also used in osteoporosis and nephrogenic DI.

renal-51.q: Which is an adverse effect of thiazides?
renal-51.e: HyperGLUC: hyperGlycemia, hyperLipidemia, hyperUricemia, hyperCalcemia; also hypokalemia, hyponatremia, metabolic alkalosis.

renal-51.q: Paradoxical use of a thiazide treats which disorder?
renal-51.e: Mild volume depletion ↑ proximal Na⁺/water reabsorption → less water reaches the collecting duct.

renal-52.q: Which K⁺-sparing diuretic directly blocks ENaC?
renal-52.e: Amiloride and triamterene block ENaC; spironolactone and eplerenone are aldosterone receptor antagonists.

renal-52.q: Gynecomastia in a man on a diuretic suggests:
renal-52.e: Spironolactone also blocks androgen receptors. Eplerenone is more selective. All K⁺-sparing agents risk hyperkalemia.

renal-52.q: Drug of choice for lithium-induced nephrogenic DI:
renal-52.e: Amiloride blocks lithium entry into principal cells via ENaC.

renal-53.e: Volume contraction (↑ AT II → NHE3) and K⁺ loss (H⁺ shifts into cells, ↑ H⁺ secretion). Acetazolamide and K⁺-sparing agents cause acidosis.

renal-53.q: Which diuretic class increases urinary NaCl and causes HYPOkalemia?
renal-53.e: Loops and thiazides deliver more Na⁺ to the collecting duct → ↑ K⁺ secretion.

renal-53.q: Thiazides cause which calcium and uric acid changes?
renal-53.e: Increased distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; reduced urate secretion.

renal-53.q: Loop diuretics cause which magnesium/calcium change?
renal-53.e: Abolishing the lumen-positive voltage reduces paracellular Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ reabsorption.

renal-54.e: GFR depends on efferent constriction by AT II; blocking it can cause AKI. Also contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal renal damage) and hereditary angioedema.

renal-54.q: Persistent dry cough on lisinopril is due to:
renal-54.e: Switch to an ARB, which does not raise bradykinin.

renal-54.q: Effect of ACE inhibitors on renin and angiotensin II:
renal-54.e: Loss of negative feedback raises renin; ACE blockade lowers AT II. Also ↓ GFR, ↑ K⁺.

renal-55.e: ARBs (-sartans) share ACE-I effects (hyperkalemia, ↓ GFR, teratogenic) but do not raise bradykinin.

renal-55.q: Compared with ACE inhibitors, ARBs are less likely to cause:
o: Acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis
renal-55.e: Angioedema can still occur but is rarer.

renal-55.q: ARBs differ from ACE inhibitors because they do not increase:

renal-56.e: Blocks conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ↓ AT II and aldosterone.

renal-56.q: Aliskiren should be avoided with ACE inhibitors or ARBs in patients with:
renal-56.e: Combining RAAS blockers raises risk of hyperkalemia, hypotension and AKI.
Direct renin inhibitor blocks angiotensinogen → Ang I.

renal-56.q: A notable adverse effect of aliskiren is:

kub-embryology:s1.q: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the collecting ducts, calyces, renal pelvis and ureter?
kub-embryology:s1.e: The ureteric bud (outgrowth of the mesonephric duct) forms the collecting system: collecting ducts → calyces → pelvis → ureter.

kub-embryology:s1.q: Metanephric mesenchyme normally forms which part of the nephron?
kub-embryology:s1.e: Reciprocal induction with the ureteric bud makes the metanephric mesenchyme form glomerulus → PCT → loop of Henle → DCT.

kub-embryology:s1.q: Which part of the ureter is the last to canalize and the most common site of congenital obstruction?
kub-embryology:s1.e: The UPJ canalizes last; incomplete canalization is the most common pathologic cause of prenatal hydronephrosis.

kub-embryology:s2.q: The pronephros appears in week 4 and:
kub-embryology:s2.e: Rudimentary, cervical, regresses by end of week 4.

kub-embryology:s2.q: The nephric (mesonephric/Wolffian) duct grows caudally to open into the:
kub-embryology:s2.e: It later gives off the ureteric bud near its cloacal end.

kub-embryology:s3.q: A stillborn infant has pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened nose, low-set ears and clubbed feet. What is the trigger of this sequence?
kub-embryology:s3.e: Potter sequence: oligohydramnios compresses the fetus → limb and facial deformities and pulmonary hypoplasia (cause of death).

kub-embryology:s3.q: Which of the following can cause Potter sequence?
o: Unilateral renal agenesis with a normal contralateral kidney
kub-embryology:s3.e: Anything that cuts fetal urine output (bilateral agenesis, ARPKD, posterior urethral valves) or amniotic fluid (PPROM, placental insufficiency) causes it.

kub-embryology:s3.q: The primary cause of the flattened face and limb deformities in Potter sequence is:
kub-embryology:s3.e: Lack of fetal urine → oligohydramnios → compression and pulmonary hypoplasia.

kub-embryology:s3.q: The usual cause of death in Potter sequence is:
kub-embryology:s3.e: Amniotic fluid is needed for lung development.

kub-embryology:s3.q: Unilateral renal agenesis results from failure of which structure to develop?
kub-embryology:s3.e: Without the ureteric bud the metanephric mesenchyme is never induced, so that kidney does not form. Often found incidentally.

kub-embryology:s3.q: A patient with unilateral renal agenesis usually shows which finding in the remaining kidney?
kub-embryology:s3.e: The solitary kidney hypertrophies; these patients have a higher risk of hyperfiltration injury later.

kub-embryology:s3.q: The ureteric bud normally induces which tissue to form nephrons?
kub-embryology:s3.e: Reciprocal induction between ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme.

kub-embryology:s4.q: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is caused by:
o: Abnormal interaction between the ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme
Obstruction at the ureterovesical junction in adults
kub-embryology:s4.e: MCDK is a nonfunctional kidney of cysts and connective tissue from failed induction; it is usually unilateral and non-inherited.

kub-embryology:s4.q: A newborn has a unilateral flank mass of noncommunicating cysts with no function on imaging. Prognosis is good when:
kub-embryology:s4.e: Unilateral MCDK with a normal other kidney carries an excellent prognosis; bilateral disease leads to Potter sequence.

kub-embryology:s4.q: Unlike ARPKD, multicystic dysplastic kidney is usually:
kub-embryology:s4.e: MCDK is usually unilateral, sporadic, with a normal opposite kidney.

kub-embryology:s4.q: MCDK results from abnormal interaction between:
kub-embryology:s4.e: Failed induction yields noncommunicating cysts and dysplastic stroma.

kub-embryology:s4.q: A duplex collecting system arises from:
o: Bifurcation of the ureteric bud before it enters the metanephric blastema
kub-embryology:s4.e: Bifid ureter or two ureters drain one kidney. It is strongly associated with vesicoureteral reflux and ureterocele.

kub-embryology:s4.q: In a complete duplex system, which ureter (Weigert–Meyer rule) typically obstructs?
o: Upper-pole ureter, inserting ectopically and inferomedially
kub-embryology:s4.e: Upper pole: inserts low and medial and tends to obstruct (ureterocele). Lower pole: inserts higher and laterally and tends to reflux.

kub-embryology:s4.q: A bifid (partially duplicated) ureter results from:
o: Early splitting of a single ureteric bud
kub-embryology:s4.e: Early division of one bud gives a Y-shaped ureter; two buds give complete duplication.

kub-embryology:s4.q: In a complete duplex system, the upper-pole ureter typically:
o: Inserts ectopically inferomedially and tends to obstruct (ureterocele)
kub-embryology:s4.e: Weigert–Meyer rule: upper pole obstructs, lower pole refluxes.

kub-embryology:s5.q: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into:
kub-embryology:s5.e: Anterior urogenital sinus, posterior anorectal canal.

kub-embryology:s5.q: The trigone of the bladder is initially derived from:

o: Urachal fistula with urine leaking from the umbilicus

kub-embryology:s6.q: During ascent, a horseshoe kidney gets trapped beneath which structure?
kub-embryology:s6.e: The fused inferior poles hook under the IMA, so the kidney stays low in the abdomen.

kub-embryology:s6.q: Horseshoe kidney is classically associated with which chromosomal disorder?
kub-embryology:s6.e: Associated with Turner syndrome and trisomies 13, 18 and 21; raises risk of hydronephrosis, stones, infection and some tumors.

kub-embryology:s6.q: Horseshoe kidney most often fuses at the:
kub-embryology:s6.e: Lower poles fuse; ascent stops at the inferior mesenteric artery.

kub-embryology:s6.q: A complication more common with horseshoe kidney is:
kub-embryology:s6.e: Abnormal ureter course predisposes to obstruction, infection and stones; also Wilms tumor risk.

kub-embryology:s7.q: Fetal urine begins to be produced at about:
kub-embryology:s7.e: Glomeruli start functioning around week 10–12; urine contributes to amniotic fluid.

kub-embryology:s7.q: Nephron formation (nephrogenesis) is complete by about:
kub-embryology:s7.e: No new nephrons form after ~34–36 weeks; kidneys grow by enlarging.

kub-embryology:s8.q: Posterior urethral valves occur only in:
kub-embryology:s8.e: A membrane remnant in the posterior (prostatic) urethra obstructs outflow in boys, the most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in male infants.

kub-embryology:s8.q: Prenatal ultrasound of a male fetus shows a thick-walled bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis and oligohydramnios. Most likely cause:
kub-embryology:s8.e: Outlet obstruction → bladder hypertrophy, bilateral hydronephrosis and low fetal urine (risk of Potter sequence).

kub-embryology:s8.q: Posterior urethral valves are best diagnosed after birth by:
kub-embryology:s8.e: VCUG shows a dilated posterior urethra and valve leaflets.

kub-embryology:s8.q: Posterior urethral valves arise in the:
kub-embryology:s8.e: Membranous folds in the posterior (prostatic) urethra obstruct outflow.

kub-anatomy:wall.e: It shares this insertion with iliacus (iliopsoas).
Psoas major is supplied by anterior rami of L1–L3.
Inferiorly to the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament.

kub-anatomy:wall.q: The psoas major is innervated by:
kub-anatomy:wall.e: Direct branches from lumbar anterior rami.

kub-anatomy:loc.q: Between which vertebral levels do the kidneys normally lie?
kub-anatomy:loc.e: Retroperitoneal on the posterior abdominal wall, T12–L3; the right kidney sits slightly lower.

kub-anatomy:loc.q: Why does the right kidney usually lie lower than the left?
o: The spleen pushes the left kidney up
The right renal artery is shorter
kub-anatomy:loc.e: The large right lobe of the liver displaces the right kidney inferiorly.

kub-anatomy:loc.q: The hilum of the left kidney lies at about the level of:

kub-anatomy:rel.q: Which structure contacts the anterior surface of the right kidney directly, without peritoneum between them?
kub-anatomy:rel.e: The duodenum is retroperitoneal; the liver and small intestine are separated from the kidney by peritoneum.

kub-anatomy:rel.q: Moving medial to lateral, which muscle is the most lateral posterior relation of the kidney?
kub-anatomy:rel.e: Posteriorly: diaphragm above, then psoas major → quadratus lumborum → transversus abdominis.

kub-anatomy:rel.q: Which nerve passes posterior to the kidney on quadratus lumborum?
The left kidney is related anteriorly to all EXCEPT:
kub-anatomy:rel.e: The second part of the duodenum lies anterior to the right kidney.

kub-anatomy:fascia.q: What is the correct order of the coverings from the kidney outward?
o: Renal fascia → renal capsule → perirenal fat → pararenal fat
Perirenal fat → renal capsule → pararenal fat → renal fascia
Renal capsule → perirenal fat → renal fascia → pararenal fat
Renal capsule → pararenal fat → renal fascia → perirenal fat
kub-anatomy:fascia.e: Pararenal (paranephric) fat lies outside the renal (Gerota) fascia, mostly posterior and posterolateral.

kub-anatomy:fascia.q: Relative to the renal fascia, the suprarenal gland is:
o: Outside it, in the pararenal fat
Inside it, separated from the kidney by a thin septum
kub-anatomy:fascia.e: So a ptotic kidney can drop without taking the suprarenal gland with it.

o: Between renal fascia and peritoneum/posterior abdominal wall
kub-anatomy:fascia.e: Perirenal fat is inside the renal fascia.
Infection or fluid may track inferiorly into the pelvis.

kub-anatomy:struct.q: From anterior to posterior, what is the order of structures at the renal hilum?
o: Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis
Renal pelvis, renal artery, renal vein
Renal vein, renal pelvis, renal artery
Renal artery, renal vein, renal pelvis
kub-anatomy:struct.e: VAP: vein anterior, artery in the middle, pelvis posterior.

kub-anatomy:struct.q: Minor calyces receive urine directly from the:
o: Papillary ducts opening on a renal papilla
kub-anatomy:struct.e: Several minor calyces unite into a major calyx; 2–3 major calyces form the renal pelvis.

kub-anatomy:struct.q: The renal pelvis forms by the union of:
The left renal vein crosses between the aorta and which artery, where it can be compressed (nutcracker syndrome)?
kub-anatomy:struct.e: The left renal vein passes between the SMA and aorta; it also receives the left gonadal and left adrenal veins.

kub-anatomy:struct.q: Why is the left kidney usually chosen for living-donor transplant?
o: It sits lower than the right
kub-anatomy:struct.e: The left renal vein is longer (crosses the aorta), which makes anastomosis easier.

kub-anatomy:struct.q: Which renal region is most sensitive to hypoxic injury?
o: Straight segment of PT and thick ascending limb in the outer medulla
kub-anatomy:struct.e: These segments have high metabolic demand and low O₂ supply, so ischemia hits them first (ATN).

kub-anatomy:vessels.q: Which renal vessel passes posterior to the inferior vena cava?
kub-anatomy:vessels.e: The right renal artery is longer and runs behind the IVC; the long left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta.

kub-anatomy:vessels.q: Which tributary drains into the left renal vein but not the right?
o: Inferior phrenic vein only on the right
kub-anatomy:vessels.e: The left gonadal and left suprarenal veins join the left renal vein; on the right they enter the IVC directly.

kub-anatomy:vessels.q: Why does occlusion of a segmental renal artery cause infarction of that segment?
o: They drain into the vasa recta
They anastomose freely with lumbar arteries
kub-anatomy:vessels.e: There are no effective anastomoses between segments.

kub-anatomy:lnn.q: Lymph from the kidneys drains mainly to:
kub-anatomy:lnn.e: Along the renal vessels to para-aortic nodes.

kub-anatomy:lnn.q: Kidney pain is referred to the loin and groin because visceral afferents enter the cord at about:
kub-anatomy:lnn.e: Sympathetic afferents with the renal plexus enter T10–L1.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three normal sites of ureteric narrowing?
o: Pelvic brim over the iliac vessels
Where the gonadal vessels cross the ureter
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Stones commonly lodge at the UPJ, pelvic brim and ureterovesical junction.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: In women, the pelvic ureter passes directly beneath the:
o: Ovarian artery in the broad ligament
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: 'Water under the bridge'; at risk during hysterectomy. In men the ductus deferens crosses above it.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: Ureteric colic is referred to dermatomes:
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Loin to groin: flank, pubic region, scrotum/labia majora, anterior thigh.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: Vesicoureteral reflux is primarily due to:
o: Short intramural segment of the ureter in the bladder wall
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: A short, laterally placed ureteric insertion lacks the flap-valve effect, so urine refluxes; it predisposes to recurrent UTI and pyelonephritis.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: A child with recurrent pyelonephritis is investigated for reflux. The diagnostic test of choice is:
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: VCUG shows contrast refluxing up the ureters during voiding; chronic VUR causes renal scarring (chronic pyelonephritis).

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: Reflux is prevented normally because the ureter:
o: Passes obliquely through the bladder wall
Has a sphincter of skeletal muscle
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Bladder pressure compresses the intramural segment.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: The main long-term risk of untreated VUR is:
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Recurrent pyelonephritis scars the kidney → hypertension and CKD.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: In the pelvis, the ureter passes under which structures ("water under the bridge")?
o: Internal iliac vein and obturator nerve
External iliac artery and femoral nerve
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: Ureters run retroperitoneally under the gonadal vessels, over the iliacs, and under the uterine artery / vas deferens.

kub-anatomy:ureter.q: During hysterectomy, the ureter is most at risk when ligating the:
o: Ovarian artery in the infundibulopelvic ligament only
kub-anatomy:ureter.e: The ureter lies ~2 cm lateral to the cervix, just beneath the uterine artery, so it can be clamped or ligated with it.

kub-anatomy:adrenal.q: The left suprarenal vein drains into the:
kub-anatomy:adrenal.e: The right suprarenal vein is very short and enters the IVC directly.

kub-anatomy:adrenal.q: The middle suprarenal artery arises from the:
kub-anatomy:adrenal.e: Superior from the inferior phrenic, middle from the aorta, inferior from the renal artery.

kub-anatomy:adrenal.q: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are innervated by:
o: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers that have not synapsed
Postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the celiac ganglion
kub-anatomy:adrenal.e: The medulla acts like a modified sympathetic ganglion.

kub-anatomy:aorta.q: At which vertebral level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate?
kub-anatomy:aorta.e: The bifurcation lies about 2.5 cm below the umbilicus, level with the iliac crests.

kub-anatomy:aorta.q: The renal arteries arise from the aorta at about:
kub-anatomy:aorta.e: The left is usually slightly higher; the right is longer.

o: Anterior to the aorta at L4
Anterior to L1–L2, posterior and to the right of the aorta
In the posterior mediastinum at T8
kub-anatomy:aorta.e: It receives the intestinal and lumbar trunks and begins the thoracic duct.

kub-anatomy:plexus.q: Which branch of the lumbar plexus emerges on the anterior surface of psoas major?
kub-anatomy:plexus.e: Medial border: obturator and lumbosacral trunk; lateral border: iliohypogastric, ilio-inguinal, LFCN, femoral.

kub-anatomy:plexus.q: Which nerve emerges from the medial border of psoas major and passes through the obturator foramen?
kub-anatomy:plexus.e: It supplies the medial thigh muscles and skin.

kub-anatomy:plexus.q: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve arises from:
kub-anatomy:plexus.e: It runs under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS; compression causes meralgia paresthetica.

kub-anatomy:bladder.q: Where is the bladder mucosa smooth and firmly attached to the muscle coat?
kub-anatomy:bladder.e: Elsewhere the mucosa is folded (rugae) and loosely attached.

kub-anatomy:bladder.q: The median umbilical ligament is the remnant of the:
kub-anatomy:bladder.e: It runs from the bladder apex to the umbilicus. The medial umbilical ligaments are the obliterated umbilical arteries.

kub-anatomy:bladder.q: Lymph from the base of the bladder drains mainly to the:
kub-anatomy:bladder.e: Superior and inferolateral surfaces → external iliac; neck → sacral nodes.

kub-anatomy:urethra.q: What is the longest part of the male urethra?
kub-anatomy:urethra.e: Spongy ~15 cm, prostatic 3–4 cm, preprostatic ~1 cm, membranous ~0.5 cm.

kub-anatomy:urethra.q: The ejaculatory ducts open onto the:
o: Seminal colliculus of the prostatic urethra
kub-anatomy:urethra.e: The prostatic utricle opens in the middle of the colliculus with an ejaculatory duct on each side.

kub-anatomy:urethra.q: Which part of the male urethra is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter in the deep perineal pouch?
kub-anatomy:urethra.e: The internal (smooth) sphincter is at the preprostatic part.

kub-anatomy:clinic.q: The left gonadal vein drains into the:
kub-anatomy:clinic.e: Left renal vein compression (nutcracker) or left RCC may cause left varicocele.

kub-anatomy:clinic.q: During hysterectomy the ureter is at risk where it passes:
o: Under the uterine artery ('water under the bridge')
kub-anatomy:clinic.e: Classic site of iatrogenic ureter injury.

kub-histology:lowpower.q: On a low-power kidney section, a pale striated band runs from the medulla into the cortex but contains no renal corpuscles. What is it?
kub-histology:lowpower.e: Medullary rays are straight tubules (proximal and distal straight parts, collecting tubules) extending into the cortex; corpuscles are absent there.

kub-histology:lowpower.q: Which zone of the renal medulla contains only thin limbs of Henle and collecting ducts?
kub-histology:lowpower.e: Inner medulla = thin limbs (of juxtamedullary nephrons) + large collecting ducts; thick limbs end at the inner–outer medulla border.

o: One medullary ray with the cortical tissue around it
One minor calyx and its papilla
One pyramid and its cortical cap
kub-histology:lowpower.e: Lobe = pyramid + overlying cortex. Lobule = a medullary ray + surrounding cortex drained by one collecting duct system.

kub-histology:lowpower.q: The sieve-like tip of a renal papilla where papillary ducts open is called:
kub-histology:lowpower.e: Openings of the papillary ducts (ducts of Bellini) give the papilla tip a perforated appearance: the area cribrosa.

kub-histology:nephron.e: Different embryologic origins: metanephric blastema and ureteric bud.

kub-histology:nephron.q: Which segment has simple squamous epithelium?
kub-histology:nephron.e: Thin limbs are squamous; TAL and DCT are cuboidal.

kub-histology:vessels.q: Blood in the arcuate arteries flows next into:
kub-histology:vessels.e: Interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole.

kub-histology:vessels.q: Vasa recta arise from efferent arterioles of:
kub-histology:vessels.e: Juxtamedullary efferents form long straight loops alongside Henle loops; cortical efferents form peritubular capillaries.

kub-histology:vessels.q: Calcium oxalate stones often start as Randall plaques in the basement membrane of:
kub-histology:vessels.e: Randall plaques form in the basement membranes of the thin limbs in the medulla.

kub-histology:vessels.q: Sickle cell disease classically injures the renal papilla because:
o: Vasa recta have low O₂ tension and high osmolality
kub-histology:vessels.e: Hypoxic, hypertonic medulla promotes sickling in the vasa recta → papillary necrosis.

kub-histology:corpuscle.q: The parietal layer of Bowman capsule is lined by:
kub-histology:corpuscle.e: Parietal layer = simple squamous; it becomes cuboidal at the urinary pole where the PCT begins.

kub-histology:corpuscle.q: Inside a glomerulus on H&E, nuclei that bulge into the urinary space on the outer surface of capillary loops belong to:
kub-histology:corpuscle.e: Podocytes cover the outer (urinary) surface of the loops. Mesangial nuclei sit centrally between loops; endothelial nuclei are flat on the inner side.

kub-histology:corpuscle.q: The urinary pole of a renal corpuscle is where:
o: The macula densa contacts the arterioles
Filtrate drains into the proximal convoluted tubule
kub-histology:corpuscle.e: Vascular pole = arterioles; urinary (tubular) pole = capsular space opens into the PCT.

kub-histology:barrier.q: A boy has hematuria, hearing loss and lens dislocation with a COL4A5 mutation. Which structure is abnormal on EM?
kub-histology:barrier.e: Alport syndrome: type IV collagen defect → split, laminated GBM.

kub-histology:barrier.q: Which protein forms the zipper-like slit diaphragm between pedicels?
kub-histology:barrier.e: Nephrin molecules from adjacent foot processes interlock; mutations cause congenital nephrotic syndrome.

kub-histology:barrier.q: The negatively charged layers of the GBM that repel anionic proteins are the:
kub-histology:barrier.e: Both laminae rarae (and the endothelial glycocalyx) carry negative charge; the lamina densa filters mainly by size.

kub-histology:barrier.q: Approximately what fraction of plasma entering a glomerulus is filtered?

kub-histology:mesangium.q: Which function is NOT performed by intraglomerular mesangial cells?
o: Production of matrix to support capillaries
kub-histology:mesangium.e: Renin comes from juxtaglomerular (granular) cells of the afferent arteriole, not mesangial cells.

kub-histology:mesangium.q: Extraglomerular mesangial cells are also called:
kub-histology:mesangium.e: Lacis cells fill the space between the afferent and efferent arterioles and the macula densa, forming part of the JGA.

o: Between capillary loops where podocytes are absent
In the wall of the efferent arteriole
kub-histology:mesangium.e: They support capillaries on surfaces not covered by podocytes, sharing a basement membrane with the endothelium.

kub-histology:pctdct.q: Compared with the PCT, the DCT in cross-section shows:
o: Taller cells with a dense brush border
Pale cells with sharp cell borders
Squamous cells with RBCs in the lumen
Smaller, paler cells, more nuclei and a clear wide lumen
kub-histology:pctdct.e: DCT: smaller, less eosinophilic cells, no brush border, more nuclei per section, empty lumen.

kub-histology:pctdct.q: Why do PCT cells stain so eosinophilic?
kub-histology:pctdct.e: Mitochondria aligned in basal infoldings power Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and give strong acidophilia.

kub-histology:pctdct.q: Which stain best highlights the PCT brush border and basement membranes in magenta?
kub-histology:pctdct.e: PAS stains the glycoprotein-rich glycocalyx of microvilli and basement membranes.

kub-histology:pctdct.q: Why are PCT sections more numerous than DCT sections in the cortex?
o: The DCT lies in the medulla
The DCT is destroyed during fixation
The PCT has more cells per section
kub-histology:pctdct.e: The PCT is the longest segment, so it is cut more often around corpuscles.

kub-histology:pctem.q: Small proteins filtered at the glomerulus are handled in the PCT by:
o: Secretion back to the capillary as protein
kub-histology:pctem.e: Apical pits and vesicles take up proteins; lysosomes degrade them and amino acids exit basolaterally.

kub-histology:pctem.q: Basal membrane infoldings packed with mitochondria indicate:
kub-histology:pctem.e: This pattern marks cells doing active transport (PCT, TAL, DCT, striated ducts).

kub-histology:pctem.q: Leaky tight junctions in the PCT allow:
o: Paracellular movement of water and solutes

kub-histology:pctem.q: The PCT stains intensely eosinophilic in H&E because of:

kub-histology:medulla.q: In the medulla, how is a thin limb of Henle told apart from a vasa recta capillary?
o: Thin limb has a brush border
Vasa recta is lined by cuboidal cells
Thin limb epithelium is slightly thicker and its lumen lacks RBCs
kub-histology:medulla.e: Both are squamous, but capillaries are thinner and usually contain erythrocytes.

kub-histology:medulla.q: Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin), the matrix of urinary casts, is made by:
kub-histology:medulla.e: Only the TAL epithelium produces Tamm-Horsfall protein.

kub-histology:medulla.q: Which segment is permeable to water but relatively impermeable to NaCl?
kub-histology:medulla.e: Thin descending limb lets water leave into the hyperosmotic interstitium; the ascending limbs are water-tight.

kub-histology:jga.q: Renin-containing granular cells of the JGA are modified:
o: Smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole
Endothelial cells of the efferent arteriole
kub-histology:jga.e: JG cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the tunica media of the afferent arteriole.

kub-histology:jga.q: Macula densa cells are distinguished on a slide by:
o: Tall, crowded cells with apically placed nuclei
kub-histology:jga.e: Macula densa: closely packed columnar cells of the distal tubule with apical nuclei and basal Golgi.
Macula densa = chemoreceptor for luminal NaCl (tubuloglomerular feedback); JG cells act as baroreceptors.

kub-histology:cd.q: An antibody to aquaporin-2 would stain which cells most intensely after ADH?
kub-histology:cd.e: ADH inserts AQP2-containing vesicles into the apical membrane of principal cells.

kub-histology:cd.q: Collecting duct cells are recognized on H&E by:
o: Pale cytoplasm and distinct cell borders
Strong eosinophilia and a brush border
kub-histology:cd.e: Principal cells have few organelles (pale) and sharp lateral borders, unlike the interdigitating tubule cells.
α-intercalated cells secrete H⁺; β-intercalated cells secrete HCO₃⁻. Both are darker and mitochondria-rich.

kub-histology:slideid.q: A medullary tubule with pale cells and sharp cell borders is most likely a:
kub-histology:slideid.e: Principal cells have few organelles and distinct lateral borders.

kub-histology:slideid.q: A thin-walled medullary profile containing red blood cells is a:
kub-histology:slideid.e: Thin limbs look similar but lack RBCs.

kub-histology:urothelium.q: Plaques of uroplakin in the apical membrane of umbrella cells serve to:
o: Form an osmotic barrier and let the surface fold and unfold
kub-histology:urothelium.e: Rigid uroplakin plaques joined by hinges fold into vesicles when empty and unfold when full, keeping the barrier intact.

kub-histology:urothelium.q: When the bladder fills, the urothelium:
o: Thins from about 5–7 to 2–3 cell layers with flattened umbrella cells
kub-histology:urothelium.e: Cells shift laterally and flatten; full urothelium can mimic stratified squamous.

kub-histology:urothelium.q: Which part of the urinary system has epithelial membranes with stiffened protein plaques?
kub-histology:urothelium.e: Umbrella cells of the bladder urothelium carry uroplakin plaques.

kub-histology:ureter.q: The muscularis of the upper two-thirds of the ureter is arranged as:
kub-histology:ureter.e: Upper ureter: inner longitudinal + outer circular; an outer longitudinal layer is added in the lower third.

kub-histology:ureter.q: Which epithelium lines the prostatic urethra?
kub-histology:ureter.e: Prostatic urethra = urothelium; membranous and spongy = stratified/pseudostratified columnar; distal end = stratified squamous.

kub-histology:ureter.q: The superior surface (dome) of the bladder is covered by:
kub-histology:ureter.e: Only the dome is covered by peritoneum (serosa); elsewhere adventitia.

kub-histology:ureter.q: A ureter in cross-section has a star-shaped lumen because:
o: The mucosa folds longitudinally when the lumen is empty
kub-histology:ureter.e: Longitudinal mucosal folds form when the undistended ureter contracts.

kub-histology:bladder.q: The detrusor muscle is arranged as:
o: Inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal
kub-histology:bladder.e: Layers intermingle except near the bladder neck.

kub-histology:bladder.q: Only the superior surface of the bladder has a:

kub-histology:urethra.q: The female urethra is lined proximally by urothelium and distally by:
The membranous urethra in males passes through the:

kub-histology:clinical.q: In acute pyelonephritis neutrophils accumulate especially in the:
kub-histology:clinical.e: Ascending infection reaches the papilla first.

renal-ch25:balance.q: Normal daily insensible water loss is about:
Water formed by metabolism adds about:
renal-ch25:balance.e: From oxidation of carbohydrates; total intake ~2300 mL/day.

renal-ch25:balance.q: During prolonged heavy exercise in heat, the largest water loss is through:

renal-ch25:compartments.q: Using the 60-40-20 rule, what fraction of body weight is extracellular fluid?
renal-ch25:compartments.e: Total body water ≈ 60% of weight; ICF 40%, ECF 20% (interstitial ¾, plasma ¼).

renal-ch25:compartments.q: Which substance is used to measure extracellular fluid volume?
renal-ch25:compartments.e: Inulin stays in the ECF. Albumin/Evans blue mark plasma; tritiated water marks total body water.

renal-ch25:compartments.q: In a 70-kg man, interstitial fluid volume is about:
renal-ch25:compartments.e: ECF 14 L = interstitial ~11 L + plasma ~3 L.

renal-ch25:compartments.q: Intracellular fluid volume is calculated as:

renal-ch25:composition.q: Plasma has slightly higher cation concentration than interstitial fluid because of:
o: Gibbs–Donnan effect of negatively charged plasma proteins

renal-ch25:measure.e: These bind albumin and stay in plasma.

renal-ch25:measure.q: Interstitial fluid volume is calculated as:
If 100 mg of a substance distributes evenly to 7.1 mg/L, its volume of distribution is about:

renal-ch25:osmosis.q: Each mOsm/L concentration gradient produces about how much osmotic pressure?
renal-ch25:osmosis.e: At 282 mOsm/L the potential pressure exceeds 5400 mmHg.

renal-ch25:osmosis.q: A cell placed in a hypotonic solution will:

renal-ch25:shifts.q: Two liters of 3% NaCl are infused into a 70-kg man. After osmotic equilibrium, which is true?
o: ECF volume increases and ICF volume decreases
renal-ch25:shifts.e: Hypertonic saline raises ECF osmolarity, pulling water out of cells: ECF ↑, ICF ↓ (Guyton: ECF 19 L, ICF 25 L, 313.9 mOsm/L).
Isotonic fluid stays in the ECF; no osmotic gradient forms across cell membranes.

renal-ch25:shifts.q: Why does 5% dextrose behave like free water after infusion?
renal-ch25:shifts.e: Glucose enters cells and is metabolized, so the net effect is adding solute-free water.

renal-ch25:shifts.q: Plasma osmolarity can be estimated at the bedside mainly from:
renal-ch25:shifts.e: Na⁺ and its anions account for most ECF osmoles: osmolarity ≈ 2 × [Na⁺].

renal-ch25:shifts.q: A solute that crosses cell membranes freely (urea) at the same osmolarity as plasma is:
renal-ch25:shifts.e: Tonicity depends on impermeant solutes; urea equilibrates across membranes, so cells eventually swell.

renal-ch25:natremia.e: Excess ADH retains water → ECF and ICF expand with low Na⁺ (Table 25-4).

renal-ch25:natremia.q: Chronic hyponatremia should be corrected slowly to avoid:
renal-ch25:natremia.e: Guyton: limit correction to <10–12 mmol/L in 24 h and <18 mmol/L in 48 h.

renal-ch25:natremia.q: The total safety factor against edema is about:
renal-ch25:natremia.e: Low compliance 3 + lymph flow 7 + protein washdown 7 ≈ 17 mmHg.

renal-ch25:natremia.q: Edema in nephrotic syndrome is mainly due to:
renal-ch25:natremia.e: Loss of albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, increasing net filtration into tissues.

renal-ch25:edema.q: Which is NOT a cause of increased capillary filtration?
renal-ch25:edema.e: Low (not high) plasma proteins cause edema.

renal-ch25:edema.q: Lymphatic obstruction from filariasis causes edema because:
renal-ch25:edema.e: Lymph cannot return protein and fluid.

renal-ch25:edema.q: Fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity is called:

renal-ch26:overview.q: Which kidney cell type makes erythropoietin in response to hypoxia?
renal-ch26:overview.e: EPO comes from peritubular interstitial cells. CKD → normocytic anemia.

renal-ch26:overview.q: 1α-hydroxylase, which makes calcitriol, is located in the:
renal-ch26:overview.e: PTH stimulates and FGF23 inhibits PCT 1α-hydroxylase; CKD → ↓ calcitriol.

renal-ch26:overview.q: During prolonged fasting, the kidney contributes to plasma glucose via:
renal-ch26:overview.e: Guyton lists renal gluconeogenesis as a kidney function.

renal-ch26:micturition.q: The micturition reflex is mediated by sensory and motor fibers in the:
renal-ch26:micturition.e: Parasympathetic pelvic nerves (S2–S3); pudendal supplies the external sphincter.

renal-ch26:micturition.q: On a cystometrogram, pressure rises sharply after bladder volume exceeds about:

o: Spinal cord lesion above sacral levels
Destruction of sensory fibers from the bladder
renal-ch26:micturition.e: e.g., crush injury of sacral roots, tabes dorsalis → overflow incontinence.

renal-ch26:urineform.e: The four processes of urine formation.

renal-ch26:urineform.q: A substance filtered and also secreted, like PAH, is excreted at a rate:
If tubular reabsorption fell by 10% with GFR unchanged, urine volume would rise from 1.5 L/day to about:

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Loss of which component of the glomerular filtration barrier best explains selective albuminuria?
o: Negative charge of the basement membrane
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Heparan sulfate gives the GBM its negative charge, which repels albumin. Loss of charge (e.g., minimal change disease) lets albumin through.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Podocyte foot processes are linked by slit diaphragms containing which protein?
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Nephrin (NPHS1) mutations cause congenital nephrotic syndrome.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Which layer of the barrier filters mainly by size?
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Laminae rarae and glycocalyx provide charge selectivity.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Albumin is restricted from filtration mainly because of its:
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Albumin (6 nm) is smaller than pores (~8 nm) but repelled by negative charges.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Which substance gives the most accurate measurement of GFR?
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted. Creatinine slightly overestimates GFR because a little is secreted.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Creatinine clearance overestimates GFR because creatinine is:
renal-ch26:gfr.e: A small amount is secreted, so clearance > true GFR by roughly 10–20%.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: If GFR falls to 50% of normal, steady-state plasma creatinine will:
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Creatinine excretion = GFR × Pcr; with constant production Pcr doubles.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Constriction of the efferent arteriole (e.g., by angiotensin II) has what effect?
o: ↑ RPF, ↑ GFR, no change in FF
↓ RPF, ↓ GFR, no change in FF
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure (↑ GFR) while reducing plasma flow, so FF = GFR/RPF rises.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: A patient takes high-dose NSAIDs. What happens at the afferent arteriole?
o: Constriction from loss of prostaglandins → ↓ RPF and ↓ GFR
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole; NSAIDs remove this and can precipitate AKI, especially with ACE inhibitors and diuretics.

renal-ch26:gfr.q: Ureteral obstruction changes GFR mainly by:
renal-ch26:gfr.e: Back-pressure raises P(BS), opposing filtration and lowering GFR.

renal-ch26:rbf.q: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts which vessel?
renal-ch26:rbf.e: Efferent constriction helps maintain GFR when arterial pressure or volume is low.

renal-ch26:rbf.q: NSAIDs can precipitate acute kidney injury in volume-depleted patients because they block:
o: Prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole
renal-ch26:rbf.e: Prostaglandins buffer vasoconstriction; blocking them lowers RBF and GFR.

renal-ch26:rbf.q: The kidneys receive about what fraction of cardiac output?
renal-ch26:rbf.e: RBF ≈ 1100 mL/min, about 22% of cardiac output.

o: Constriction of renal arterioles and decreased GFR
renal-ch26:rbf.e: Intense sympathetic stimulation constricts renal arterioles, lowering RBF and GFR.

renal-ch26:autoreg.q: GFR and RBF are autoregulated over a mean arterial pressure range of about:
renal-ch26:autoreg.e: Autoregulation keeps GFR and RBF relatively constant between ~75 and 160 mmHg.

renal-ch26:autoreg.q: Decreased NaCl at the macula densa causes:
o: Afferent dilation and increased renin release
renal-ch26:autoreg.e: Tubuloglomerular feedback dilates the afferent arteriole and stimulates renin → Ang II constricts the efferent.
Stretch opens Ca²⁺ channels in vascular smooth muscle → contraction, limiting transmitted pressure.

renal-ch26:autoreg.q: A high-protein meal increases GFR because:
o: More Na⁺ is reabsorbed with amino acids in the PCT, so less NaCl reaches the macula densa
renal-ch26:autoreg.e: Reduced macula densa NaCl triggers TGF-mediated afferent dilation.

renal-ch27:transport.q: At what plasma glucose concentration does glucose first appear in urine (threshold)?
renal-ch27:transport.e: Glucosuria begins ~200 mg/dL; SGLT transporters are fully saturated (Tm) ~375 mg/dL.

renal-ch27:transport.q: Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule mainly by:
renal-ch27:transport.e: SGLT2 in the early PCT reabsorbs most glucose; SGLT2 inhibitors (-gliflozins) cause glucosuria.

renal-ch27:transport.q: Pregnancy commonly causes glucosuria at normal plasma glucose because:
o: ↑ GFR raises filtered load and ↓ proximal reabsorption
Placental hormones block SGLT1 in the gut
Insulin resistance raises plasma glucose above 375
renal-ch27:transport.e: Higher GFR and reduced proximal reabsorption during pregnancy lower the effective threshold.

renal-ch27:transport.q: The transport maximum for glucose is about:
renal-ch27:transport.e: Tm ≈ 375 mg/min; filtered load at normal plasma glucose ≈ 125 mg/min.

renal-ch27:transport.q: Glucose appears in urine before Tm is reached because of:
o: Splay: nephrons differ in Tm and filtered load
renal-ch27:transport.e: Threshold (~200 mg/min) is below Tm because not all nephrons saturate together.

renal-ch27:transport.q: SGLT2 in the PCT is an example of:
renal-ch27:transport.e: Glucose rides the Na⁺ gradient created by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.

renal-ch27:transport.q: Proteins filtered at the glomerulus are reabsorbed in the PCT by:
renal-ch27:transport.e: Pinocytosis at the brush border, then lysosomal digestion.

renal-ch27:pct.q: The PCT reabsorbs about what fraction of filtered Na⁺ and water?
Along the PCT, the TF/P ratio of inulin rises because:
o: Water is reabsorbed while inulin remains

renal-ch27:pct.q: Organic anions such as penicillin and PAH are secreted in the:
renal-ch27:pct.e: Organic anion transporters on the basolateral membrane.

renal-ch27:loop.q: Which segment reabsorbs about 25% of filtered Na⁺ but is impermeable to water?
renal-ch27:loop.e: The TAL (NKCC2) is the diluting segment.

renal-ch27:loop.q: The lumen-positive potential in the TAL drives paracellular reabsorption of:
renal-ch27:loop.e: K⁺ back-leak through ROMK makes the lumen ~+8 mV, pushing cations between cells.

renal-ch27:loop.q: Principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct:
renal-ch27:loop.e: ENaC and ROMK under aldosterone control; water permeability needs ADH.

renal-ch27:loop.q: The early distal tubule NaCl co-transporter is blocked by:

renal-ch27:distal.q: Aldosterone acts on principal cells to:
o: Increase Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion

renal-ch27:distal.q: The medullary collecting duct is permeable to urea:

renal-ch27:segments.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs most of the filtered Na⁺, glucose, amino acids, and HCO₃⁻?
renal-ch27:segments.e: The early PCT is the 'workhorse': ~65–80% of Na⁺ and water and nearly all glucose and amino acids.

renal-ch27:segments.q: Which segment is impermeable to water and is the 'diluting segment' that builds medullary hypertonicity?
o: Inner medullary collecting duct with ADH
renal-ch27:segments.e: The TAL reabsorbs Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ without water, so tubular fluid becomes dilute.

renal-ch27:segments.q: Principal cells of the collecting duct reabsorb Na⁺ through:
renal-ch27:segments.e: Aldosterone ↑ ENaC and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in principal cells, also ↑ K⁺ secretion. ADH inserts AQP2.

renal-ch27:regulation.q: PTH acts on the kidney to:
o: ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the DCT and ↓ phosphate reabsorption in the PCT
renal-ch27:regulation.e: PTH: ↑ Ca²⁺ (DCT), ↓ PO₄³⁻ (blocks NaPi in PCT), ↑ 1α-hydroxylase.

renal-ch27:regulation.q: ADH increases water reabsorption by binding which receptor on principal cells?
renal-ch27:regulation.e: V2 → cAMP → AQP2 insertion in the collecting duct. V1 mediates vasoconstriction.

renal-ch27:regulation.q: ANP released from atrial stretch causes:
o: Afferent dilation, efferent constriction and ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → natriuresis
renal-ch27:regulation.e: ANP/BNP → ↑ GFR and natriuresis; 'aldosterone escape' in primary hyperaldosteronism.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: The renal clearance of substance X is greater than GFR. This means X is:
renal-ch27:clearance.e: Cx > GFR → secretion; Cx < GFR → reabsorption; Cx = GFR → filtered only.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: Ux = 100 mg/mL, V = 1 mL/min, Px = 2 mg/mL. Clearance of X is:
Clearance of a substance that is filtered and completely reabsorbed is:
renal-ch27:clearance.e: Glucose at normal plasma level has clearance ~0.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: Clearance of inulin is 125 mL/min and of urea 70 mL/min. This indicates urea is:
renal-ch27:clearance.e: Clearance below GFR means net reabsorption.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: Effective renal plasma flow is estimated using the clearance of:
renal-ch27:clearance.e: PAH is filtered and secreted almost completely in one pass; it slightly underestimates true RPF.

renal-ch27:clearance.q: ERPF = 600 mL/min and hematocrit = 40%. Renal blood flow is about:
PAH clearance underestimates true renal plasma flow by about:

renal-ch28:dilute.q: Without ADH, urine osmolarity can fall to about:
renal-ch28:dilute.e: Distal segments keep reabsorbing solute but not water.

renal-ch28:dilute.q: Tubular fluid at the end of the ascending limb is about:

renal-ch28:concreq.q: The two requirements for forming concentrated urine are:
o: High ADH and a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium
Low ADH and low medullary osmolarity

renal-ch28:concreq.q: Urine specific gravity rises by 0.001 for every increase in osmolarity of about:

o: Its salt load (~1200 mOsm/L) exceeds what the kidney can concentrate
renal-ch28:concreq.e: Extra water must be excreted to remove the salt.

renal-ch28:countercurrent.q: The thick ascending limb can establish a gradient of about how much between lumen and interstitium?
renal-ch28:countercurrent.e: The single effect is ~200 mOsm/L; flow multiplies it to 1200–1400 at the papilla.

renal-ch28:countercurrent.q: Urea contributes to medullary hyperosmolality mainly through:
o: Passive reabsorption from inner medullary collecting ducts via UT-A1/A3
renal-ch28:countercurrent.e: ADH increases urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct.

renal-ch28:countercurrent.q: The vasa recta preserve the medullary gradient because they:
o: Act as countercurrent exchangers with low flow
renal-ch28:countercurrent.e: Hairpin loops and sluggish flow minimize washout of solute.

renal-ch28:countercurrent.q: A low-protein diet reduces maximal urine concentrating ability because:
o: Less urea is available for the medullary interstitium
renal-ch28:countercurrent.e: Urea supplies 40–50% of inner medullary osmolality.

renal-ch28:urea.q: Increased medullary blood flow tends to:
Urea moves from collecting ducts into the thin limbs, a process called:
renal-ch28:urea.e: Traps urea in the inner medulla.

renal-ch28:concentrate.q: Urine flow 2 mL/min, Uosm 150, Posm 300. Free water clearance is:
Central diabetes insipidus is distinguished from nephrogenic DI by:
renal-ch28:concentrate.e: Central DI responds to ADH analog.

renal-ch28:adh.q: ADH secretion is most sensitive to:
renal-ch28:adh.e: Osmoreceptors respond to ~1% changes; volume must fall ~10% to strongly stimulate ADH.

renal-ch28:adh.q: Free water clearance is negative when:
renal-ch28:adh.e: CH₂O = V − Cosm; concentrated urine means water is being conserved.
Alcohol and clonidine inhibit; nausea, morphine, nicotine and hypoxia stimulate.

renal-ch28:adh.q: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is caused by:
o: Failure of the kidney to respond to ADH
renal-ch28:adh.e: V2 receptor/AQP2 defects or drugs like lithium.

renal-ch28:adh.q: The obligatory urine volume in a person excreting 600 mOsm/day with maximal concentration 1200 mOsm/L is:

renal-ch29:potassium.q: Which of the following shifts K⁺ INTO cells, causing hypokalemia?
renal-ch29:potassium.e: Insulin, β-agonists, alkalosis and hypo-osmolarity shift K⁺ in. ↓ Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, acidosis and lysis shift K⁺ out.

renal-ch29:potassium.q: Digoxin toxicity can cause hyperkalemia by:
renal-ch29:potassium.e: Blocking the pump leaves K⁺ outside cells.

o: Stimulating Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase to move K⁺ into cells
renal-ch29:potassium.e: Used acutely with glucose in hyperkalemia.

renal-ch29:potassium.q: Which shifts K⁺ OUT of cells?
renal-ch29:potassium.e: Also acidosis, cell lysis and strenuous exercise.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: ECG shows peaked T waves, wide QRS and arrhythmia risk. The electrolyte disturbance is:
renal-ch29:capimg.e: Hypokalemia gives U waves and flat T waves; hypocalcemia prolongs QT.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia risks:
renal-ch29:capimg.e: Correcting hyponatremia too fast causes osmotic demyelination ('from low to high, your pons will die'). Correcting hypernatremia too fast causes cerebral edema.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: Hypomagnesemia makes hypokalemia refractory because Mg²⁺ normally:
o: Inhibits ROMK K⁺ secretion in the distal nephron
renal-ch29:capimg.e: Low Mg²⁺ removes the brake on ROMK, so renal K⁺ wasting continues until Mg²⁺ is replaced.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: About what fraction of plasma calcium is ionized (the physiologically active form)?
renal-ch29:capimg.e: ~50% ionized, ~40% bound to plasma proteins, ~10% complexed with anions; ionized + complexed are filterable.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: Which diuretic decreases urinary Ca²⁺ excretion?
renal-ch29:capimg.e: Thiazides enhance distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; loop diuretics increase calcium loss.

renal-ch29:capimg.q: Most filtered Mg²⁺ is reabsorbed in the:
renal-ch29:capimg.e: The TAL reabsorbs ~65% of filtered magnesium (paracellular).

renal-ch29:volume.q: Long-term arterial pressure is set mainly by:
renal-ch29:volume.e: Pressure settles where renal output equals intake on the renal function curve.

o: Return of Na⁺ excretion to normal despite continued aldosterone excess
renal-ch29:volume.e: Rising arterial pressure causes pressure natriuresis that offsets Na⁺ retention; hypokalemia persists.

renal-ch29:volume.q: If angiotensin II cannot be suppressed during a high-salt diet, the result is:
renal-ch29:volume.e: The renal function curve flattens; higher pressure is needed to excrete the salt.

renal-ch29:volume.q: ANP is released in response to:
renal-ch29:volume.e: ANP increases Na⁺ excretion and inhibits renin; its role is modest.

renal-ch29:raas.q: Renin is released from juxtaglomerular cells in response to all EXCEPT:
o: Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa
Decreased NaCl delivery to the macula densa
renal-ch29:raas.e: Renin rises with ↓ perfusion, β₁ stimulation and ↓ NaCl at the macula densa. ↑ NaCl delivery suppresses it.

renal-ch29:raas.q: Angiotensin II acts on the proximal tubule to:
o: ↑ Na⁺/H⁺ exchange → ↑ Na⁺, HCO₃⁻ and water reabsorption
renal-ch29:raas.e: AT II stimulates NHE3 (can cause contraction alkalosis), constricts the efferent arteriole, releases aldosterone and ADH, and drives thirst.

renal-ch29:raas.q: ACE also degrades which vasodilator, explaining cough and angioedema with ACE inhibitors?

renal-ch30:buffers.q: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 28, HCO₃⁻ 12. Expected PaCO₂ by Winter's formula is ~26 ± 2. This is:
o: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
renal-ch30:buffers.e: Winter's: 1.5(12) + 8 = 26 ± 2; measured 28 is within range, so compensation is appropriate.

renal-ch30:buffers.q: Which causes a HIGH anion gap metabolic acidosis?
renal-ch30:buffers.e: MUDPILES-type causes (methanol, uremia, DKA, propylene glycol, iron/INH, lactate, ethylene glycol, salicylates). Diarrhea, RTA, acetazolamide → normal AG.

renal-ch30:buffers.q: Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis that is maintained by:
o: Volume contraction → ↑ aldosterone and AT II
renal-ch30:buffers.e: Loss of HCl and volume; RAAS keeps HCO₃⁻ reabsorption high (saline-responsive alkalosis).

renal-ch30:resp.q: Doubling alveolar ventilation raises pH by about:
Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis is incomplete because:
o: Stimulus fades as pH approaches normal
Urine pH > 5.5 and hypokalemia with calcium phosphate stones
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: Defect in α-intercalated cell H⁺ secretion; causes include amphotericin B, analgesic nephropathy, autoimmune disease.
Hyperkalemia ↓ ammoniagenesis → ↓ acid excretion; urine pH < 5.5. Causes: diabetes (hyporeninemic), ACE-I, ARBs, K⁺-sparing diuretics.
Defective PCT HCO₃⁻ reabsorption; urine pH < 5.5 once plasma HCO₃⁻ is depleted. Hypokalemia.

renal-ch30:renalacid.q: The kidneys must reabsorb about how much HCO₃⁻ per day?
New HCO₃⁻ is added to the blood when secreted H⁺ combines with:
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: Titratable acid and ammonium excretion generate new bicarbonate.

renal-ch30:renalacid.q: In chronic acidosis, the most adaptable renal mechanism is:
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: NH₄⁺ production can rise from ~50 to ~500 mEq/day.

renal-ch30:renalacid.q: Primary active H⁺ secretion that can lower urine pH to 4.5 occurs in:
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: H⁺-ATPase and H⁺/K⁺-ATPase create a ~900-fold gradient.

o: Increased H⁺ secretion and metabolic alkalosis
renal-ch30:renalacid.e: Table 30-2: hypokalemia stimulates H⁺ secretion and HCO₃⁻ reabsorption.

renal-ch30:ammonia.q: In the PCT, each glutamine metabolized yields:
renal-ch30:ammonia.e: NH₄⁺ to lumen, new HCO₃⁻ to blood.
Each unit generates one new HCO₃⁻.

renal-ch30:ammonia.q: Titratable acid mainly reflects H⁺ bound to:
renal-ch30:ammonia.e: Measured by titrating urine back to pH 7.4.

renal-ch30:abd.q: Which disorder causes hypertension with ↑ renin and ↑ aldosterone?
renal-ch30:abd.e: Low renal perfusion activates RAAS. Primary hyperaldosteronism has ↑ aldosterone but ↓ renin.

renal-ch30:abd.q: Hypertension with ↑ aldosterone and ↓ renin suggests:
renal-ch30:abd.e: Autonomous aldosterone suppresses renin; hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis are common.
Reduced perfusion → renin ↑ → Ang II and aldosterone ↑.

o: Hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin and low aldosterone
renal-ch30:abd.e: ENaC gain of function mimics hyperaldosteronism with suppressed RAAS.

renal-ch31:diuretics.q: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act mainly in the:

o: Competing with aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor

renal-ch31:diuretics.q: The natriuretic effect of a diuretic diminishes after a few days because:
o: Reduced ECF volume activates compensatory Na⁺ retention

renal-ch31:aki.q: Prerenal acute kidney injury is caused by:
In ATN the tubular epithelium can regenerate in 10–20 days if:
A life-threatening effect of anuria lasting more than a few days is:
renal-ch31:aki.e: Death can occur within 8–14 days without treatment.

renal-ch31:ckd.q: The two leading causes of end-stage renal disease are:
The 'vicious cycle' of CKD is driven by:
o: Hyperfiltration and increased glomerular pressure in surviving nephrons
renal-ch31:ckd.e: Surviving nephrons hypertrophy; glomerular hypertension leads to sclerosis.

renal-ch31:ckd.q: Anemia in CKD is mainly due to:
Isosthenuria in advanced CKD means urine osmolality is fixed near:
renal-ch31:ckd.e: Remaining nephrons can neither dilute nor concentrate well.

o: Reduced 1,25-(OH)₂D₃ and phosphate retention with secondary hyperparathyroidism

renal-ch31:tubular.q: A child has hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypercalciuria and normal BP. The defect affects which transporter?
o: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb (Bartter)
renal-ch31:tubular.e: Bartter mimics loop diuretics: hypokalemic alkalosis with HYPERcalciuria.

renal-ch31:tubular.q: Hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia and HYPOcalciuria point to:
renal-ch31:tubular.e: Gitelman = NCC defect in the DCT, mimicking thiazides (hypocalciuria). It is milder than Bartter.

renal-ch31:tubular.q: Hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis with LOW aldosterone that responds to amiloride:
renal-ch31:tubular.e: Gain-of-function ENaC (↓ degradation) → Na⁺ retention with suppressed renin and aldosterone. Treat with amiloride.

renal-ch31:tubular.q: Generalized PCT reabsorption defect with glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and type 2 RTA is:
renal-ch31:tubular.e: Causes include Wilson disease, ifosfamide, cisplatin, expired tetracyclines, multiple myeloma and lead.

harrison-ch321:aki-dx.q: RBC casts in the urine point to:
harrison-ch321:aki-dx.e: RBC casts = glomerular bleeding (nephritic syndrome, vasculitis, malignant hypertension).

harrison-ch321:aki-dx.q: Muddy brown granular casts are characteristic of:
harrison-ch321:aki-dx.e: Granular casts come from sloughed tubular cells. Waxy (broad) casts suggest advanced CKD. WBC casts suggest pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis.

harrison-ch321:aki-dx.q: WBC casts distinguish acute pyelonephritis from:
harrison-ch321:aki-dx.e: Casts form in tubules, so they indicate upper-tract (renal) inflammation, not bladder infection.

o: Hematuria with RBC casts and hypertension
Proteinuria > 3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia and edema
robbins-ch20:glomresp.e: Nephritic = inflammation (hematuria, RBC casts, HTN, azotemia). Nephrotic = podocyte damage (massive proteinuria).

robbins-ch20:glomresp.q: Nephrotic patients are hypercoagulable mainly because they lose:
robbins-ch20:glomresp.e: Urinary antithrombin loss → thrombosis risk (e.g., renal vein thrombosis, especially in membranous nephropathy).

o: Hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension and oliguria
robbins-ch20:glomresp.e: Inflammation damages the GBM, letting RBCs through.

robbins-ch20:glomresp.q: 'Spike and dome' on EM with subepithelial deposits suggests:

robbins-ch20:psgn.q: Two weeks after impetigo, a 7-year-old has cola-colored urine and periorbital edema. Complement shows:
robbins-ch20:psgn.e: Poststreptococcal GN is immune complex–mediated with ↓ C3; most children recover fully.

robbins-ch20:psgn.q: Anti-GBM antibodies against type IV collagen α3 with linear IF and hemoptysis is:
robbins-ch20:psgn.e: Type II hypersensitivity; linear IgG on IF; RPGR with pulmonary hemorrhage.

robbins-ch20:psgn.q: Gross hematuria 1–2 days after a URI with mesangial IgA deposits is:
robbins-ch20:psgn.e: Synpharyngitic hematuria (days, not weeks). Most common GN worldwide; related to IgA vasculitis.

robbins-ch20:psgn.q: Hereditary nephritis with sensorineural deafness and lens dislocation is:
robbins-ch20:psgn.e: Type IV collagen defect (often X-linked); 'basket-weave' GBM splitting on EM. Can't see, can't pee, can't hear a bee.

robbins-ch20:nephrotic.q: Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children; EM shows effaced foot processes and light microscopy is normal:
robbins-ch20:nephrotic.e: Selective albuminuria, excellent response to corticosteroids; may follow infection, vaccine or Hodgkin lymphoma.

robbins-ch20:nephrotic.q: Anti-PLA2R antibodies with spike-and-dome subepithelial deposits indicate:
robbins-ch20:nephrotic.e: Most common primary nephrotic cause in white adults. Secondary causes: SLE, hepatitis B/C, NSAIDs, solid tumors.

robbins-ch20:nephrotic.q: Nephrotic syndrome in a patient with HIV, heroin use or sickle cell disease is most likely:
robbins-ch20:nephrotic.e: FSGS: segmental sclerosis; most common primary nephrotic cause in Black and Hispanic adults. HIV causes the collapsing variant.

robbins-ch20:stones.q: The most common type of kidney stone is:
robbins-ch20:stones.e: Calcium stones (oxalate > phosphate) are most common; risks include hypercalciuria and low citrate.

robbins-ch20:stones.q: Staghorn calculi in alkaline urine with a urease-positive organism are made of:
robbins-ch20:stones.e: Proteus, Klebsiella, Staph saprophyticus split urea → NH₃ → alkaline urine. Treat infection and remove stone.

robbins-ch20:stones.q: Radiolucent stones forming in acidic urine in a patient with gout or tumor lysis are:
robbins-ch20:stones.e: Not visible on X-ray (visible on CT/US); treat with urine alkalinization and allopurinol.

robbins-ch20:stones.q: Hexagonal crystals and a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test indicate:
robbins-ch20:stones.e: Cystinuria (defective COLA transporter in PCT) — treat with alkalinization, hydration, chelating agents.

robbins-ch20:obstruction.q: Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces most often due to:
robbins-ch20:obstruction.e: Causes: stones, BPH, cervical cancer, PUV, pregnancy. Prolonged pressure causes cortical atrophy.

robbins-ch20:obstruction.q: Bilateral hydronephrosis in an older man with nocturia and weak stream suggests:
robbins-ch20:obstruction.e: Bladder outlet obstruction affects both kidneys; unilateral hydronephrosis suggests an obstruction above the bladder.

robbins-ch20:obstruction.q: Unilateral hydronephrosis from a stone usually:
o: Leaves creatinine near normal because the other kidney compensates
robbins-ch20:obstruction.e: Bilateral obstruction or a single kidney is needed for renal failure.

o: Compression atrophy of the cortex and medulla
robbins-ch20:obstruction.e: Pressure transmitted back damages renal parenchyma.

robbins-ch21:cystitis.q: The most common cause of acute cystitis is:
robbins-ch21:cystitis.e: E. coli is most common; S. saprophyticus is the second most common cause in sexually active young women.

robbins-ch21:cystitis.q: A positive leukocyte esterase test indicates:
robbins-ch21:cystitis.e: Nitrite test detects gram-negative bacteria (nitrate reductase). Sterile pyuria suggests urethritis (Chlamydia, gonorrhea).
E. coli and other Enterobacteriaceae convert nitrate to nitrite.
WBCs without growth on standard culture.

robbins-ch21:cystitis.q: A renal transplant recipient has yellow mucosal plaques in the bladder; macrophages contain laminated calcified Michaelis–Gutmann bodies. Diagnosis:
robbins-ch21:cystitis.e: Malakoplakia: defective phagolysosome function in chronic E. coli infection, more frequent in immunosuppression.
Cytotoxic drugs (cyclophosphamide) and adenovirus/BK virus cause hemorrhagic cystitis.

robbins-ch21:cystitis.q: The main purpose of biopsy in suspected interstitial cystitis is to:

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness and WBC casts indicate:
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Upper-tract infection, usually ascending E. coli; affects cortex with relative glomerular sparing.

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Chronic pyelonephritis shows coarse asymmetric corticomedullary scarring and thyroidization of the kidney due to:
o: Recurrent infection with reflux or obstruction
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Tubules contain eosinophilic casts resembling thyroid follicles.

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Chronic pyelonephritis with thyroid-like tubules filled with eosinophilic casts is called:
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is classically associated with:
Sloughing of renal papillae with gross hematuria is associated with all EXCEPT:
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: SAAD papa: Sickle cell, Acute pyelonephritis, Analgesics, Diabetes.

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Papillary necrosis is particularly likely because the papillae have:
o: Poor blood supply from vasa recta in a hypertonic environment
Direct arterial supply from interlobar arteries
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Low O₂ and hypertonicity make the papillae vulnerable (e.g., sickling).

robbins-ch20:pyelo.q: Causes of renal papillary necrosis include:
o: Sickle cell, diabetes, analgesic abuse, pyelonephritis
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Mnemonic SAAD: Sickle cell, Acute pyelonephritis, Analgesics, Diabetes.

o: Gross hematuria and flank pain, possibly sloughed papillae in urine
robbins-ch20:pyelo.e: Sloughed papilla may cause ureteric obstruction.

harrison-ch321:aki-def.q: BUN:Cr > 20 and FENa < 1% in AKI suggest:
harrison-ch321:aki-def.e: Hypoperfusion → kidneys avidly reabsorb Na⁺ and urea. Intrinsic damage gives FENa > 2% and BUN:Cr < 15.

harrison-ch321:aki-def.q: Urine osmolality > 500 mOsm/kg in AKI points to:
harrison-ch321:aki-def.e: Intact tubules still concentrate urine. ATN loses concentrating ability (Uosm < 350).
Tubules work and avidly reabsorb Na⁺ and urea.

robbins-ch20:tin.q: Fever, rash, eosinophilia and pyuria with WBC casts days after starting a drug suggest:
robbins-ch20:tin.e: Hypersensitivity to drugs (penicillins, PPIs, NSAIDs, diuretics, rifampin, sulfonamides); urine eosinophils.

robbins-ch20:tin.q: First step in managing drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis is:
robbins-ch20:tin.e: Most recover after withdrawal; corticosteroids may help if improvement is slow.

robbins-ch20:tin.q: Drugs commonly causing acute interstitial nephritis include:
robbins-ch20:tin.e: Hypersensitivity (type IV) reaction in the interstitium.

robbins-ch20:tin.q: A characteristic urine finding in drug-induced AIN is:
robbins-ch20:tin.e: Eosinophiluria and WBC casts with fever and rash.

robbins-ch20:atn.q: The most common cause of acute kidney injury in hospitalized patients is:
robbins-ch20:atn.e: Ischemic (shock, sepsis) or nephrotoxic (aminoglycosides, contrast, myoglobin, cisplatin) ATN.

robbins-ch20:atn.q: The maintenance phase of ATN is notable for:
o: Oliguria with hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis
robbins-ch20:atn.e: Recovery phase: tubules regenerate → polyuria and risk of hypokalemia.
High O₂ demand in the outer medulla.
Direct tubular toxicity; basement membrane usually preserved so cells regenerate.

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Which consequence of CKD causes a normocytic anemia?
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: CKD: ↓ EPO → anemia; also uremia, HTN, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, renal osteodystrophy.

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Uremia can cause which complication requiring urgent dialysis?
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: Dialysis indications (AEIOU): Acidosis, Electrolytes (K⁺), Intoxication, Overload, Uremic symptoms (pericarditis, encephalopathy).

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Uremic pericarditis is an indication for:
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: Dialysis indications: AEIOU (acidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, overload, uremia).

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Hyperkalemia in kidney failure occurs because:
The primary cause of anemia in CKD is:
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: Normocytic anemia from stage 3, almost universal by stage 4.

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: The leading cause of death in CKD is:
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: CVD is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality.

harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.q: Before starting an ESA in CKD you should ensure:
harrison-ch322:ckd-sys.e: Iron (TSAT, ferritin) is needed for response.

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: Renal osteodystrophy develops because CKD causes:
o: ↓ Calcitriol and phosphate retention → secondary hyperparathyroidism
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: Hypocalcemia + hyperphosphatemia + ↓ vitamin D → ↑ PTH → bone resorption (osteitis fibrosa cystica).

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: In CKD-mineral bone disease, FGF23 is:
o: Increased, lowering calcitriol and promoting phosphaturia
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: Osteocyte FGF23 rises early to excrete phosphate and inhibits 1α-hydroxylase.

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD is driven by:
o: Phosphate retention, low calcitriol and hypocalcemia

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: Osteitis fibrosa cystica in CKD is due to:
In CKD, the earliest hormonal change in mineral metabolism is a rise in:
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: FGF-23 rises early in response to phosphate retention.

harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.q: Adynamic bone disease is associated with:
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: Low turnover bone disease, increasingly common in diabetics and the elderly.

o: Vascular calcification with skin necrosis, almost exclusively in advanced CKD
harrison-ch322:ckd-mbd.e: A devastating condition in ESKD patients.

robbins-ch20:cystic.q: Bilateral enlarged kidneys with cysts, hematuria and flank pain in an adult with a family history and berry aneurysms:
robbins-ch20:cystic.e: PKD1 (chr 16) or PKD2 (chr 4). Associations: berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, hepatic cysts, diverticulosis. Tolvaptan slows progression.

robbins-ch20:cystic.q: ARPKD presents in infancy and is associated with:
robbins-ch20:cystic.e: PKHD1 mutation; can cause Potter sequence; survivors develop portal hypertension and hypertension.
PKD1/PKD2 mutations; also mitral valve prolapse.

robbins-ch20:cystic.q: Acquired cystic kidney disease is seen in:
robbins-ch20:cystic.e: Risk of renal cell carcinoma rises.

robbins-ch20:rcc.q: Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell) arises from which cells?
robbins-ch20:rcc.e: Polygonal clear cells filled with lipid and carbohydrate; associated with VHL gene deletion on chromosome 3.

robbins-ch20:rcc.q: Classic triad of RCC (rarely all present):
o: Hematuria, palpable flank mass and flank pain
robbins-ch20:rcc.e: RCC can secrete EPO (polycythemia), PTHrP (hypercalcemia), renin, ACTH; it may invade the IVC and cause left varicocele.

robbins-ch20:rcc.q: Strongest modifiable risk factor for RCC:
robbins-ch20:rcc.e: Also obesity, male sex, hypertension; von Hippel–Lindau → bilateral RCC.

robbins-ch20:benign.q: A renal mass with a central stellate scar and large eosinophilic cells full of mitochondria is:
robbins-ch20:benign.e: Benign tumor from collecting duct intercalated cells; usually removed because it is hard to tell from RCC on imaging.
Benign tumor of intercalated cells, mitochondria-rich.

robbins-ch20:benign.q: On histology, oncocytes are eosinophilic because they contain many:
robbins-ch20:benign.e: Packed mitochondria give granular pink cytoplasm.

robbins-ch20:benign.q: Management of a suspected oncocytoma is usually:
robbins-ch20:benign.e: Hard to distinguish from chromophobe RCC preoperatively.

robbins-ch20:wilms.q: Most common renal malignancy of early childhood presenting as a large palpable unilateral flank mass:
robbins-ch20:wilms.e: Ages 2–4; contains embryonic glomerular structures; loss of WT1 or WT2 (chromosome 11).

robbins-ch20:wilms.q: WAGR syndrome includes Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies and:
robbins-ch20:wilms.e: WT1 deletion. Beckwith–Wiedemann (WT2): macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihyperplasia. Denys–Drash: early nephropathy, DSD.

robbins-ch20:wilms.q: Wilms tumor histology shows a triphasic pattern of:
o: Small round cells with rosettes only

robbins-ch20:wilms.q: WT1 mutations in Denys–Drash syndrome cause Wilms tumor plus:
o: Early nephrotic syndrome (mesangial sclerosis) and male pseudohermaphroditism

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma most commonly presents with:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Can occur anywhere from pelvis to bladder; often multifocal and recurrent.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Which exposure is most strongly linked to urothelial carcinoma?
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Also aromatic amines (dyes, rubber), cyclophosphamide, phenacetin. Schistosomiasis is linked to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Cyclophosphamide increases the risk of bladder cancer via:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Also causes hemorrhagic cystitis; prevented by mesna.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder is associated with:
The most important risk factor for urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Smoking raises risk 3–7×; 50–80% of bladder cancers in men are smoking-associated.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Non-muscle-invasive papillary urothelial tumors commonly carry:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: Papillary pathway: FGFR3/RAS/PI3K; frequent recurrence but only ~20% progress to muscle invasion.

robbins-ch21:urothelial.q: Most muscle-invasive bladder cancers arise from:
robbins-ch21:urothelial.e: CIS pathway with early TP53/RB mutations gives rise to most muscle-invasive cancers.

robbins-ch20:syndromes.q: A patient has BUN and creatinine elevated with nausea, peripheral neuropathy and fibrinous pericarditis. This is best termed:
robbins-ch20:syndromes.e: Uremia = azotemia plus clinical signs and biochemical abnormalities (uremic gastroenteritis, neuropathy, fibrinous pericarditis).

robbins-ch20:syndromes.q: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is defined clinically by:
o: Nephritic syndrome with rapid decline in GFR over days–weeks
robbins-ch20:syndromes.e: RPGN = nephritic picture + rapid GFR loss; morphologically crescents in most glomeruli.

robbins-ch20:immune.q: Linear IgG along the GBM on immunofluorescence indicates antibodies against:
o: α3 NC1 domain of type IV collagen
robbins-ch20:immune.e: Anti-GBM disease: in situ antibodies against the α3 chain NC1 domain of type IV collagen produce a linear pattern.

robbins-ch20:immune.q: Why do subepithelial deposits cause little inflammation compared with subendothelial deposits?
o: The GBM separates them from circulating leukocytes
They are cleared by mesangial cells
robbins-ch20:immune.e: Subepithelial deposits sit outside the GBM, away from blood leukocytes, so proteinuria dominates (e.g., membranous).

robbins-ch20:immune.q: Membranous nephropathy in most primary cases is due to autoantibodies against:
robbins-ch20:immune.e: Primary MN: in situ immune complexes with podocyte antigen PLA2R (70–80%), less often THSD7A.

robbins-ch20:progression.q: The histologic feature that best predicts decline of GFR in chronic glomerular disease is:
robbins-ch20:progression.e: Tubulointerstitial fibrosis correlates better with loss of renal function than the severity of glomerular injury.

robbins-ch20:progression.q: ACE inhibitors slow progression of CKD mainly by:
o: Reducing intraglomerular pressure via efferent dilation
robbins-ch20:progression.e: Adaptive hyperfiltration raises glomerular capillary pressure; ACEi/ARB dilate the efferent arteriole and lower it.

robbins-ch20:rpgn.q: Pauci-immune crescentic GN is most often associated with:
robbins-ch20:rpgn.e: Type III (pauci-immune) RPGN: little or no Ig on IF; >90% of idiopathic cases are ANCA-positive (GPA = PR3, MPA = MPO).

o: Parietal epithelial cells and monocytes/macrophages, driven by fibrin
robbins-ch20:rpgn.e: Fibrin leakage into Bowman space stimulates parietal cell proliferation and macrophage influx.

robbins-ch20:rpgn.q: Goodpasture syndrome differs from renal-limited anti-GBM disease by the presence of:
robbins-ch20:rpgn.e: Anti-GBM antibodies cross-react with alveolar basement membrane → pulmonary hemorrhage.

robbins-ch20:iga.q: A 20-year-old has gross hematuria 1 day after a sore throat. Biopsy will most likely show:
robbins-ch20:iga.e: Synpharyngitic hematuria = IgA nephropathy; mesangial IgA ± C3. PSGN appears 1–4 weeks later.

robbins-ch20:iga.q: The key abnormal molecule in IgA nephropathy is:
robbins-ch20:iga.e: Galactose-deficient IgA1 elicits autoantibodies forming immune complexes that deposit in the mesangium.

robbins-ch20:iga.q: Henoch–Schönlein purpura shares its renal lesion with:
robbins-ch20:iga.e: HSP (IgA vasculitis) has mesangial IgA deposition identical to IgA nephropathy plus purpura, GI and joint symptoms.

robbins-ch20:alport.q: A boy with hematuria, sensorineural deafness and lens dislocation most likely has a mutation in:
robbins-ch20:alport.e: Alport syndrome: ~85% X-linked COL4A5; GBM shows splitting/basket-weave.

robbins-ch20:alport.q: Thin basement membrane nephropathy typically presents with:
o: Persistent asymptomatic hematuria with normal renal function
robbins-ch20:alport.e: Benign familial hematuria: heterozygous COL4A3/A4, GBM 150–250 nm, normal function.

robbins-ch20:membranous.q: Silver stain showing 'spikes' along the GBM is characteristic of:
robbins-ch20:membranous.e: GBM material grows between subepithelial deposits, forming spikes.

robbins-ch20:membranous.q: A patient with membranous nephropathy develops sudden flank pain and hematuria. The most likely complication is:
robbins-ch20:membranous.e: Nephrotic syndrome (especially MN) is hypercoagulable: loss of antithrombin III → renal vein thrombosis.

robbins-ch20:membranous.q: Which is a cause of secondary membranous nephropathy?
o: Hepatitis B and carcinoma of lung/colon
robbins-ch20:membranous.e: Secondary MN: HBV, HCV, syphilis, malaria, solid tumors, SLE, NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold.

robbins-ch20:mcd.q: A 4-year-old with nephrotic syndrome; LM normal, IF negative. EM shows:
robbins-ch20:mcd.e: Minimal change disease: only EM change is diffuse foot process effacement.

robbins-ch20:mcd.q: Minimal change disease in adults is classically associated with:
robbins-ch20:mcd.e: MCD is linked to Hodgkin lymphoma, NSAIDs, atopy, recent URI or vaccination.

robbins-ch20:mcd.q: The best predictor of good prognosis in childhood nephrotic syndrome is:
robbins-ch20:mcd.e: >90% of children with MCD respond to steroids; relapses may occur but prognosis is excellent.

robbins-ch20:fsgs.q: Collapsing glomerulopathy with tubular microcysts is classically seen in:
robbins-ch20:fsgs.e: HIVAN: collapsing variant of FSGS with podocyte hyperplasia and microcystic tubules.

robbins-ch20:fsgs.q: APOL1 risk variants increase the risk of FSGS in people of:
robbins-ch20:fsgs.e: APOL1 variants on chromosome 22 are common in African ancestry and raise risk of FSGS and nondiabetic CKD.

robbins-ch20:fsgs.q: Compared with minimal change disease, FSGS more often shows:
o: Hematuria, hypertension and poor steroid response
robbins-ch20:fsgs.e: FSGS: nonselective proteinuria, hematuria, HT, poor steroid response, ~50% ESRD in 10 years.

robbins-ch20:mpgn.q: 'Tram-track' double contour of capillary walls results from:
o: Mesangial interposition and new basement membrane
robbins-ch20:mpgn.e: In MPGN, mesangial cells extend into the capillary wall and lay down new BM → duplicated contour.

robbins-ch20:mpgn.q: Dense deposit disease is caused by:
o: Dysregulated alternative complement pathway (e.g., C3 nephritic factor)
robbins-ch20:mpgn.e: C3 glomerulopathy: C3NeF stabilizes C3 convertase → low C3 and C3-only deposits.

robbins-ch20:mpgn.q: Secondary immune-complex MPGN is most classically associated with:
robbins-ch20:mpgn.e: Chronic HCV (± cryoglobulins), HBV, endocarditis, SLE and CLL/lymphoma cause MPGN.

robbins-ch20:lupus.q: The most common and most severe class of lupus nephritis is:
robbins-ch20:lupus.e: Diffuse proliferative (≥50% glomeruli) with subendothelial deposits and wire loops.

robbins-ch20:lupus.q: 'Wire loop' lesions in lupus are due to:
